about: Health Pillars (the athlete, Nov 1, 2026): the Health tab's 7 pillars and their metrics. Definitions only; coach/tools/pillars.py computes values and status from data/ and coach/ files and emits pillar rows into coach.json. Weight 1-10 = how strongly the metric predicts death and major disease and how much changing it changes risk (coach judgment from the cited studies, not a validated score); 0 = context, not scored. verify: true marks a link or figure recalled from memory and not yet checked into research/LIBRARY.md. celebrate: false = never earns wins, streaks or badges (body composition: under-fuelling risk).

rules.pillar_colour: worst status among members with weight 5 or more
rules.unknown_pillar: leading metric unknown and less than half the pillar's weight known
rules.lead_override: a member with a higher weight at Act takes the lead
rules.improving: change over about 12 weeks in the good direction, larger than half the series SD and the metric's minimum step

pillars.name: Heart & fitness
pillars.what: How fit your heart and lungs are, and how much you move.

pillars.name: Checkups & labs
pillars.what: Silent risks that only a cuff or a blood test shows.

pillars.name: Habits
pillars.what: Nicotine, alcohol and food: the biggest lifestyle levers.

pillars.name: Strength & mobility
pillars.what: Muscle, balance and the ability to get up off the floor.

pillars.name: Body composition
pillars.what: Belly fat and lean mass, the drivers of diabetes risk.

pillars.name: Sleep & recovery
pillars.what: Enough sleep at regular times, and how well you bounce back.

pillars.name: Mind & connection
pillars.what: Mood, stress and the people around you.

metrics.name: Cardio fitness (VO2max)
metrics.what: How much oxygen your body can use at full effort. The watch estimates it from outdoor runs.
metrics.why: This is the strongest fitness predictor of a long life. Each step up lowers mortality, and no upper limit has been found.
metrics.target: 60th percentile for your age and sex or better (43.4 for men 30–39)
metrics.basis: Latest Garmin running estimate. There's no extra averaging because the watch already smooths it. Percentile vs FRIEND 2022 lab norms, men 30–39.

studies.finding: Elite fitness had about 80% lower mortality than the lowest fitness group.
Risk fell at every fitness level, with no point where more fitness stopped helping.

metrics.name: Activity minutes
metrics.what: Moderate minutes plus vigorous minutes counted twice.
metrics.why: 150 minutes a week cuts mortality by about a third. The benefit levels off around 2 to 4 times that.
metrics.basis: Average of the last 4 weeks: moderate minutes plus vigorous minutes counted twice, from the watch.
metrics.pop: About 1 in 4 US adults meets both the aerobic and strength guidelines.

studies.finding: 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate activity, or the vigorous equivalent.
Mortality benefit plateaued at about 3 to 5 times the guideline.

metrics.name: Resting heart rate
metrics.what: Your overnight resting heart rate, as a 28-night average.
metrics.why: A lower rate goes with lower risk. In athletes it mostly mirrors fitness, and a sudden rise flags illness or fatigue.
metrics.target: Under 55, and no 5+ bpm jump over your own baseline
metrics.basis: 28-night rolling average. The shaded band is your night-to-night spread (±1 SD).
metrics.pop: The typical adult range is 60 to 80 bpm. In athletes a low value mostly reflects fitness, so there's no percentile.

studies.finding: About 9% higher mortality for every 10 bpm higher.

metrics.name: Blood pressure
metrics.cad: Yearly check-in, home week twice a year
metrics.what: The pressure in your arteries. A 7-day home average is more reliable than one reading.
metrics.why: High blood pressure is the leading modifiable cause of death worldwide, and it has no symptoms.
metrics.basis: Your latest reported reading or home-week average. It turns Unknown after 12 months.
metrics.pop: Nearly half of US adults have high blood pressure (130/80 or above).

studies.finding: Each 20 mmHg higher systolic doubled heart and stroke death, starting from 115.
Screen adults 18+, and confirm with readings outside the clinic.

metrics.name: Cholesterol (ApoB or LDL)
metrics.what: The particles that carry cholesterol into artery walls. ApoB counts them directly.
metrics.why: Lifetime exposure to these particles is a direct cause of heart attacks. Lowering them lowers risk.
metrics.target: ApoB under 90 or LDL under 100 mg/dL, unless your clinician sets another
metrics.basis: Your latest lab value and its date. ApoB is used when you have it, LDL otherwise. It turns Unknown after 12 months.
metrics.pop: Shown against the age and sex distribution once you have a result.

studies.kind: consensus of genetic studies, cohorts and trials
studies.finding: LDL particles cause atherosclerosis, and the effect grows with years of exposure.
Lipid panel every ~5 years; ApoB for leftover risk; PREVENT risk score from age 30.

metrics.name: Lp(a), once in life
metrics.what: A genetic cholesterol particle. It's high in about 1 in 5 people.
metrics.why: A high level raises heart risk regardless of lifestyle. Knowing it changes how hard to push the other numbers.
metrics.basis: One lab value for life. It's genetic, so it never expires.
metrics.pop: About 1 in 5 people has a high level.

studies.finding: Measure at least once in every adult's life.

metrics.name: Blood sugar (A1c)
metrics.what: Your average blood sugar over about 3 months.
metrics.why: Prediabetes raises heart and diabetes risk years before any symptoms, and catching it early is when it can be reversed.
metrics.basis: Your latest lab value and its date. It turns Unknown after 12 months.
metrics.pop: About 1 in 3 US adults has prediabetes, and most don't know it.

studies.finding: A1c predicted diabetes, heart disease and death better than fasting glucose.
Screen ages 35 to 70 with overweight. Lean adults are covered by clinician judgment.

metrics.name: Physical up to date
metrics.what: A visit with standard bloodwork. It's the only way to fill the lab rows above.
metrics.why: Without it, several of the highest-weighted health metrics stay unknown.
metrics.basis: The date of your last physical, as you report it.
metrics.next: Book a physical. It fills BP, cholesterol, A1c and more.

studies.finding: The screenings with proven benefit, by age and sex.

metrics.name: Kidney and liver
metrics.what: eGFR and ALT. They're included in standard bloodwork.
metrics.why: They give a baseline before long ultras, which can strain the kidneys, and catch problems that have no symptoms.
metrics.basis: Your latest lab values and their date. They turn Unknown after 12 months.

studies.finding: Lower eGFR predicted higher mortality, independent of other risks.

metrics.name: Nicotine
metrics.what: Smoking, vaping or other nicotine.
metrics.why: Smoking costs about 10 years of life. Quitting before 40 wins back about 90% of that.
metrics.basis: Your yearly answer. You're asked monthly if you answer 'current'.
metrics.next: Talk to your clinician about quitting support.

studies.finding: Smokers lost 10+ years; quitting at 25 to 34 regained about 10.

metrics.name: Alcohol
metrics.what: Standard drinks per week (12 oz beer, 5 oz wine or 1.5 oz spirits).
metrics.why: Risk rises from about 7 drinks a week. Even 1 a day raises the risk of AFib (an irregular heart rhythm), which endurance athletes are already more prone to.
metrics.target: Under 7 a week; fewer is better
metrics.basis: Average of your last 4 weekly answers, using the middle of each range.
metrics.pop: US guidelines say 2 a day or fewer for men and 1 for women. Risk starts rising well below that.
metrics.next: Pick two alcohol-free days a week.

studies.finding: Mortality rose above about 100 g a week (about 7 US drinks).
About 1 drink a day raised AFib risk by about 16%.
Athletes had about 2.5 times the AFib odds of non-athletes.

metrics.name: Diet quality
metrics.what: A 13-item Mediterranean-style checklist (vegetables, olive oil, legumes, fish, nuts and so on): the PREDIMED 14-item score without its wine item.
metrics.why: In a randomised trial, a Mediterranean diet cut heart attacks, strokes and heart deaths by about 30%.
metrics.basis: Your latest quarterly checklist score. It turns Unknown after 4 months.
metrics.next: Add one item from the checklist this month, such as legumes 3 times a week.

studies.finding: About 30% fewer major cardiovascular events.

metrics.name: Sauna (bonus)
metrics.what: Sauna sessions per week.
metrics.why: 2+ a week went with lower mortality in one Finnish cohort. It's a bonus, not a pillar.
metrics.basis: Sessions in the last 90 days divided by 13 weeks, including ones you add in the weekly check-in.

studies.finding: 4 to 7 sessions a week went with about 40% lower mortality than 1.

metrics.name: Strength days
metrics.what: Days a week with muscle-strengthening work.
metrics.why: Two sessions a week go with 10 to 17% lower mortality, on top of what cardio gives.
metrics.basis: Days with a strength session in the last 4 weeks, divided by 4. Sessions come from the watch, the Lifts log or the weekly check-in, and a double session counts once.
metrics.pop: About 3 in 10 US adults do strength work 2+ days a week.
metrics.next: Add 15 minutes of Long Life Lifts after two easy sessions this week.

studies.finding: 10 to 17% lower mortality; the biggest gain came at 30 to 60 min a week.

metrics.name: Self-tests
metrics.what: Sit-to-rise, one-leg stand and grip. About 2 minutes each.
metrics.why: Low scores predicted mortality in middle and older age. Before 50 they're a baseline to protect.
metrics.target: All three each quarter (two if you have no grip gauge)
metrics.basis: Tests done in the last 100 days, each with its latest result.
metrics.pop: Each test is shown against its age norm once you've done it.

studies.finding: Failing a 10-second one-leg stand went with higher mortality.
Lower sit-to-rise scores predicted mortality.
Weaker grip predicted death and heart disease.

metrics.name: Waist-to-height ratio
metrics.what: Waist at the navel divided by height. It needs just a tape measure.
metrics.why: It tracks belly (visceral) fat, and it predicts diabetes and heart risk better than BMI.
metrics.basis: Your latest monthly waist measurement divided by your height. Measure on waking, at the navel, after breathing out. It turns Unknown after 6 weeks.

studies.finding: Waist-to-height beat BMI and waist alone for cardiometabolic risk.

metrics.name: Body fat %
metrics.what: From a bioimpedance scale. It can read 3 to 5 points off a lab value, so the trend matters more than the number.
metrics.why: Higher fat for your size goes with diabetes and heart risk. The trend also protects lean mass during a weight cut.
metrics.basis: 14-day average of morning scale readings (needs 4+ readings).

studies.finding: Higher body fat % predicted mortality, independent of BMI.

metrics.name: BMI
metrics.what: Weight for height. It's crude for muscular people.
metrics.why: At the population level, 20 to 25 has the lowest mortality.
metrics.basis: 7-day average weight divided by height squared.
metrics.pop: About 3 in 4 US adults are above 25.

studies.finding: Lowest mortality was at BMI 20 to 25.

metrics.name: Weight
metrics.what: Morning weigh-ins, shown against your plan when a weight goal is active.
metrics.why: It's a goal metric rather than a risk metric on its own. BMI and waist carry the risk; weight shows whether the plan is on track.
metrics.basis: 7-day average of morning weigh-ins, which is the line decisions are based on. One weigh-in never changes the plan.

studies.finding: Risk is lowest across a range of weights, not at one number.

metrics.name: Lean mass
metrics.what: Weight minus fat mass, from the scale.
metrics.why: During a weight cut, holding lean mass means you're losing fat and not muscle.
metrics.target: No drop of 2+ lb vs your baseline window
metrics.basis: 14-day average of weight × (1 − body fat %), compared with the baseline window before the deficit.

studies.finding: Muscle-strengthening work lowers mortality. Keeping muscle is the point of this guard.

metrics.name: Sleep regularity
metrics.what: How much your sleep midpoint moves from night to night.
metrics.why: Regular sleep predicted lower mortality more strongly than sleep length did.
metrics.basis: The standard deviation of your sleep midpoint over the last 28 nights. This number is itself a spread: lower means more regular.

studies.finding: The most regular fifth had about 30% lower mortality than the least regular.

metrics.name: Sleep length
metrics.what: Watch total, less about 30 minutes (watches overcount).
metrics.why: Short sleep goes with higher mortality and worse recovery.
metrics.basis: 28-night average of watch sleep minus 30 min. The shaded band is your night-to-night spread (±1 SD) on the watch figure.
metrics.pop: About 1 in 3 US adults sleeps under 7 hours.
metrics.next: Protect a fixed lights-out time on work and study nights.

studies.finding: Under 6 h had about 12% higher mortality.

metrics.name: HRV (overnight)
metrics.what: How much your heartbeat varies overnight. Higher than your own usual means well recovered.
metrics.why: It drives today's readiness. It varies so much between people that it's judged only against your own range, so it doesn't set the pillar colour.
metrics.basis: 28-night average of overnight HRV. The shaded band is your night-to-night spread (±1 SD).

studies.finding: Stress and poor recovery show up in recovery markers. HRV is used against a personal baseline.

metrics.name: Energy and legs
metrics.what: Your morning 1 to 5 answers.
metrics.why: This is how you feel compared with your own recent normal. Two mornings a full point under means back off today.
metrics.basis: Your latest daily answers against the average of the 14 days before.

studies.finding: Self-reported stress and energy tracked how fast people recovered.

metrics.name: Wellbeing (WHO-5)
metrics.what: 5 quick questions on mood, calm, energy, rest and interest.
metrics.why: Low wellbeing and depression raise heart risk and erode training. This short scale catches it early.
metrics.basis: Your latest monthly total, 0 to 25. It turns Unknown after 6 weeks.
metrics.pop: Scores under 13 suggest low wellbeing and are worth raising with a clinician.
metrics.next: Your score suggests low wellbeing. Please mention it to your clinician; exercise helps, but it's not the whole answer.

studies.finding: A valid, sensitive screen; under 13 suggests low wellbeing.
Exercise treats depression, and strength and running work best.

metrics.name: Social connection
metrics.what: A 3-question loneliness scale. Training with people counts.
metrics.why: Strong social ties went with 50% better survival odds, an effect comparable to smoking.
metrics.basis: Your latest quarterly 3-item score, 3 to 9. Lower is better. It turns Unknown after 4 months.
metrics.next: Plan one session a week with someone: a ride, a run or a class.

studies.finding: Odds of survival were 1.5 times higher with stronger relationships.

metrics.name: Stress (daily check)
metrics.what: Your 1 to 5 self-rating from the morning check.
metrics.why: High stress slows recovery from training. It shapes today's plan more than long-term risk.
metrics.basis: Average of your last 14 daily answers.

studies.finding: Higher life stress slowed recovery of strength and energy after hard sessions.
